title-group.article-title: Geometry-Anchored Features and Machine-Level Conformal Calibration for Cross-Machine Bearing Fault Diagnosis

abstract.p: Bearing fault diagnosis remains challenging when models trained on one set of machines are applied to equipment with different bearing geometries, operating speeds, and vibration characteristics. Conventional evaluation protocols often overestimate cross-machine performance, while prediction uncertainty becomes difficult to calibrate under machine-level distribution shift. This study investigates whether geometry-anchored fault features and machine-level conformal calibration can jointly improve diagnostic accuracy and prediction-set reliability on previously unseen machines. A structured review was conducted to identify methodological gaps, followed by controlled simulations involving eight machines with different bearing geometries, shaft speeds, sampling rates, structural resonances, and noise conditions. Three feature representations and four calibration schemes were evaluated using a leave-one-machine-out protocol. The geometry-anchored representation achieved a mean classification accuracy of 0.908 $\pm$ 0.014, compared with 0.585 $\pm$ 0.016 and 0.575 $\pm$ 0.023 for frequency-domain and order-domain features, respectively. Random window splitting overestimated the accuracy of these baselines by 0.25 and 0.29. At a nominal coverage level of 90%, machine-level conformal calibration achieved mean coverage between 0.903 and 0.931, compared with 0.642–0.879 for conventional split calibration. With geometry-anchored features, the calibrated prediction sets contained 0.99 classes on average, whereas the other representations required 2.77–2.96 classes. Conservative calibration increased worst-machine coverage from 0.751 to 0.866, although individual-machine coverage remained variable. The results indicate that physically indexed fault features and machine-level calibration address complementary aspects of cross-machine diagnosis: the former improves fault discrimination, while the latter supports more reliable marginal coverage under machine shift. The study establishes a controlled evaluation framework for examining diagnostic generalization and uncertainty calibration at the machine level, providing a methodological basis for subsequent validation using experimental and industrial bearing data.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Rolling-element bearings are essential components of rotating machinery, and their operating condition has a direct influence on equipment reliability, production continuity, and maintenance requirements. Vibration-based fault diagnosis has become an established application of machine learning in industrial condition monitoring, with numerous studies reporting classification accuracies approaching 100% on publicly available bearing datasets [1], [2]. Despite these results, diagnostic performance measured under benchmark conditions does not necessarily reflect the reliability of a model deployed on unfamiliar equipment. Two closely related issues are particularly important: whether the evaluation procedure adequately represents the differences between machines and whether the uncertainty associated with diagnostic predictions remains reliable when those differences arise.

The first issue concerns the unit of evaluation. Bearing vibration datasets commonly consist of long recordings divided into shorter, sometimes overlapping, signal windows. When windows from the same recording are assigned to both training and testing, a classifier may exploit recording-specific characteristics rather than learning fault patterns that generalize across equipment. Smith and Randall [3] examined the diagnostic properties of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) bearing dataset, highlighting the importance of its experimental characteristics when interpreting classification results. Hendriks et al. [4] further identified inconsistencies in dataset selection, preprocessing, and evaluation procedures that complicate comparisons between diagnostic studies. Separating recordings or operating conditions provides a more demanding evaluation than random window splitting, but it does not fully reproduce deployment on another machine. In industrial applications, the target equipment may have a different bearing geometry, rotational speed, sensor arrangement, and vibration transmission path. Evaluating generalization therefore requires the machine itself to be treated as an independent testing unit.

The second issue concerns the reliability of diagnostic uncertainty. A single predicted fault label does not indicate whether alternative diagnoses remain plausible, particularly when the target machine differs from the equipment represented during training. Conformal prediction provides a framework for constructing prediction sets with finite-sample marginal coverage under exchangeability [5], [6]. However, this assumption is generally not assured when calibration data originate from known machines and predictions are required for an unseen machine with different signal characteristics. Methods developed to address distribution shift, including weighted conformal prediction, offer possible corrections under specified assumptions [7], [8], but their application becomes difficult when source and target feature distributions have limited overlap. These difficulties connect diagnostic generalization with uncertainty calibration. Machine-dependent features may produce both inaccurate classifications and poorly calibrated prediction scores, while increasing prediction-set size to recover empirical coverage can leave several competing fault classes unresolved. Existing reviews have examined diagnostic architectures, transfer-learning methods, and their performance across operating conditions [1], [2], [9], whereas the relationship between the evaluation unit, feature representation, and prediction-set reliability has received less attention. Research combining conformal prediction with cross-domain fault diagnosis has begun to address uncertainty under distribution shift [10], but machine-specific coverage and the diagnostic informativeness of prediction sets remain important questions.
Against this background, the present study addresses four research questions (RQs):

p.p: RQ1. To what extent do conventional data-splitting protocols overestimate diagnostic accuracy on previously unseen machines, and how does feature representation affect cross-machine generalization?
RQ2. Can machine-level calibration improve the empirical coverage of prediction sets without labelled observations from the target machine, and how does this affect prediction-set size?
RQ3. How does prediction-set coverage vary across machines and fault classes, and what are the implications for unknown-fault detection and cost-sensitive diagnostic decisions?
RQ4. Which evaluation and reporting practices are needed to assess diagnostic generalization and prediction reliability under machine-level distribution shift?

sec.p: To investigate these questions, the study combines a structured narrative review with controlled simulation and analytical evaluation, as illustrated in Figure 1. The literature review in Section 2 examines the methodological foundations of cross-machine diagnosis and identifies five research gaps from which seven hypotheses are formulated. Sections 3 and 4 describe and evaluate a simulation involving eight machines with different bearing geometries, rotational speeds, sampling rates, structural resonances, and noise conditions. The experiments compare three feature representations and four conformal calibration schemes under leave-one-machine-out evaluation, allowing diagnostic performance and uncertainty calibration to be assessed on machines excluded from model development. Two complementary analytical investigations examine the ambiguity of fault frequencies across bearing configurations and the relationship between the number of source machines and machine-level coverage. Section 5 brings together the experimental findings, hypothesis assessments, and reporting recommendations.

sec.p: The study makes three principal contributions.

p.p: Machine-level evaluation and conformal calibration. A leave-one-machine-out evaluation protocol is combined with a leakage audit and a machine-level calibration procedure, termed leave-machine-out conformal prediction (LMO-CP). Calibration scores are obtained through nested machine holdouts, with each calibration machine evaluated using a model trained without its observations. The procedure is examined alongside conventional calibration schemes and conservative, class-conditional, and adaptive-score variants, allowing average coverage, machine-specific coverage, and prediction-set size to be compared within a common experimental framework.

Geometry-anchored representation for cross-machine diagnosis. A kinematic feature representation is constructed by extracting envelope-spectrum amplitudes at characteristic fault orders determined from each machine’s bearing geometry and rotational speed. Unlike features defined at fixed frequencies or fixed spectral orders, the resulting variables retain their association with specific bearing fault mechanisms across machine configurations. The representation is evaluated through feature ablation, geometric and speed perturbations, model-mismatch experiments, classifier substitution, and a structural analysis of fault-order collisions.

Joint assessment of diagnostic performance and prediction reliability. The study examines classification accuracy together with prediction-set coverage and informativeness, including differences between individual machines and fault classes. Density-ratio weighting, unknown-fault detection, and cost-sensitive abstention are also investigated to establish how uncertainty-aware diagnostic procedures behave under the simulated machine shifts. The findings are consolidated into a twelve-item reporting checklist covering evaluation protocols, calibration, robustness, and operational decision requirements.

sec.p: The methodological basis of the study draws on established developments in conformal prediction, signal processing, and transfer learning. Split conformal prediction provides the foundation for prediction-set construction [5], [6], while cross-conformal and jackknife+ methods illustrate how held-out observations can contribute to predictive inference [11], [12]. Weighted conformal prediction addresses covariate shift under assumptions concerning the relationship between source and target distributions [7]. In bearing diagnosis, envelope analysis and characteristic fault-frequency calculations provide the physical basis for identifying fault-related vibration components [13], [14], whereas domain-adaptation methods address differences between training and target distributions through learned representations or distribution alignment [15], [16], [17]. The present study brings these established elements together by aligning the feature representation and calibration procedure with the machine-level evaluation setting. Rather than treating windows as independent units of transfer, it examines the consequences of excluding entire machines from model training and calibration, while reporting prediction-set size and machine-specific coverage alongside diagnostic accuracy.

Several related studies provide useful points of comparison. Cross-domain bearing diagnosis with conformal prediction has been investigated using labelled target-domain calibration data [10], whereas the present evaluation excludes target-machine labels from calibration. Physics-informed diagnostic approaches have incorporated bearing geometry, rotational speed, and mechanical relationships into signal representations, training data, or learning constraints [18], [19], [20]. These studies establish the relevance of physical information to fault classification, but the evaluation considered here focuses specifically on the interaction between geometry-indexed features and prediction-set calibration when complete machines are held out. Recent domain-adaptation approaches have examined feature alignment across devices and operating conditions [21], [22], generally using target-domain observations during adaptation and emphasizing classification performance. Group-conditional conformal prediction provides another relevant statistical perspective by establishing coverage under specified group structures or classes of distribution shifts [23]. Its assumptions differ from those encountered when only a small number of source machines are available and the target machine contributes no labelled calibration observations. Within the literature examined in Section 2, the combined evaluation of geometry-anchored features, leave-machine-out calibration, machine-specific coverage, and prediction-set size has not been addressed as a unified diagnostic problem.

The present investigation is based on controlled simulation, which permits machine characteristics and fault mechanisms to be varied while retaining known ground truth. This design supports a systematic examination of the relationship between feature representation, machine shift, and conformal calibration. The resulting findings establish an experimental and analytical basis for assessing cross-machine diagnostic reliability and for designing subsequent evaluations using independently collected bearing vibration measurements.

sec.title: 2.1. Scope and approach
sec.p: The literature review was organized around the methodological requirements of bearing fault diagnosis on previously unseen machines. Rather than surveying diagnostic algorithms solely according to model architecture or reported classification accuracy, the review examined how existing studies defined the evaluation unit, represented fault-related vibration information, addressed differences between machines, and assessed prediction uncertainty. These considerations are closely connected in industrial applications, where the bearing configuration and operating environment of a target machine may differ from those encountered during model development.

A structured narrative synthesis was adopted to bring together three categories of research: foundational studies on bearing vibration analysis, conformal prediction, and domain adaptation; established reviews and methodological assessments of bearing diagnosis benchmarks; and recent investigations of cross-domain fault diagnosis and uncertainty quantification. The review was not conducted as a Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA)-style systematic review and did not involve a formal database screening procedure. Among the selected sources, a recent preprint examining conformal prediction under cross-dataset bearing fault diagnosis was included because of its direct relevance to the calibration problem considered here [10]. Each research thread was examined in terms of its methodological assumptions, evaluation protocol, treatment of distribution shift, and implications for diagnosis on an unseen machine. The resulting synthesis was used to identify the gaps summarized in Section 2.7. Particular attention was also given to recent studies and preprints from 2024 to 2026 concerning cross-domain transfer, physics-informed diagnostic representations, and group-aware uncertainty calibration [20], [21], [22], [23], [24].

sec.title: 2.2. Evaluation practice and the leakage problem
sec.p: The development of learning-based bearing diagnosis has been accompanied by increasingly high classification accuracies on established experimental datasets. Reviews of machine fault diagnosis have documented the extensive use of deep learning and the near-perfect performance frequently reported on benchmarks such as the CWRU dataset [1], [2]. These results must, however, be interpreted in relation to the way the experimental data are selected and divided. Smith and Randall demonstrated that individual CWRU recordings differ substantially in their diagnostic characteristics, making the choice of recordings an important factor in benchmark evaluation [3]. Hendriks et al. [4] subsequently identified considerable variation in data selection, preprocessing, and train–test splitting across studies using the same dataset, and proposed guidelines for more consistent benchmarking.

A particularly important distinction concerns whether the observations assigned to training and testing originate from independent recordings or machines. Vibration recordings are commonly divided into shorter windows, and adjacent windows may share fault signatures, background noise, operating conditions, and recording-specific characteristics. When windows from the same recording occur in both datasets, the evaluation partly measures the recognition of previously encountered signal characteristics. Separating complete recordings reduces this dependence, but the resulting test still concerns generalization within an already represented machine. A further distinction arises when operating conditions, rather than recordings, are held out. Public bearing datasets, including Paderborn [25], XJTU-SY [26], and CWRU [3], [4], have been widely used in fault diagnosis research. Transfer-learning studies have also examined diagnostic performance across changes in operating conditions and data distributions [9], [27]. Nevertheless, transferring between conditions of the same test rig differs from diagnosing faults on equipment with a different bearing geometry, sensor arrangement, and structural transmission path.

These distinctions establish a hierarchy of evaluation protocols, summarized in Table 1. Random window splitting primarily examines recognition within the available recordings, whereas recording-level separation assesses generalization to new observations from an existing machine. Condition-level holdout introduces changes in operating conditions, and machine-level holdout evaluates the ability to diagnose faults on equipment excluded from model development. Cross-dataset evaluation introduces additional differences between laboratories, acquisition systems, and experimental configurations. A recent cross-dataset investigation using convolutional neural networks reported classification accuracies of approximately 24%–36% when transferring between CWRU and Southeast University (SEU) bearing datasets [10]. Such findings illustrate the substantial dependence of reported diagnostic performance on the evaluation setting. They also indicate why machine-level separation is necessary when the intended application concerns previously unseen equipment.

sec.title: 2.3. Feature representations for cross-machine diagnosis
sec.p: The transferability of a diagnostic model depends not only on the learning algorithm but also on whether its input features retain consistent physical meaning across machines. Classical bearing diagnosis identifies fault-related components in the envelope spectrum, often after selecting a suitable resonance band using spectral kurtosis. Characteristic fault frequencies are calculated from the bearing geometry and rotational speed, allowing the measured spectral response to be interpreted in relation to specific mechanical fault mechanisms [13], [14]. This approach establishes a direct connection between the feature location and the physical source of the vibration.

Many learning-based diagnostic methods instead use raw vibration signals, conventional spectra, or time-frequency representations as model inputs [1], [2], [28]. Such representations can retain substantial information about fault-related patterns, but the classifier must learn how those patterns correspond to fault categories under different operating and machine configurations. Other studies have retained more of the physical structure during feature construction or model development. For example, cyclic spectral coherence has been combined with convolutional neural networks for bearing fault classification [18], while dynamic bearing models have been used to generate training data for operating conditions in which measured fault samples are unavailable [19]. These approaches demonstrate alternative ways of incorporating mechanical information into data-driven diagnosis. Their evaluation settings, however, differ from the machine-level holdout and uncertainty-calibration framework considered in this study.

Order-domain representations provide an intermediate approach by expressing spectral frequency relative to shaft rotational frequency. This transformation reduces the dependence of fault signatures on rotational speed, but characteristic bearing fault orders remain functions of bearing geometry. Differences in rolling-element number, diameter ratio, and contact angle can therefore cause the same order to correspond to different faults on different machines. Conversely, the same fault mechanism may appear at different orders when bearing geometry changes. These relationships are examined through the structural fault-order analysis in Section 4.15.

Recent physics-informed learning approaches have sought to incorporate these mechanical relationships more directly. A multimodal convolutional framework, for example, introduced constraints associated with ball-pass frequencies calculated from bearing geometry and rotational speed, and examined diagnostic transfer across operating conditions and datasets [20]. This approach uses fault-frequency relationships to constrain a learned model, whereas the geometry-anchored representation investigated here extracts spectral information directly at the calculated fault orders. The distinction concerns how physical knowledge enters the diagnostic process. The related studies discussed above [18], [19] provide a basis for physically informed diagnosis, while the present work examines whether explicitly indexed fault features retain their diagnostic meaning when complete machines are excluded from training.

sec.title: 2.4. Domain adaptation and cross-machine generalization
sec.p: Differences between machines are commonly treated as a domain-shift problem. Domain-adaptation methods attempt to reduce discrepancies between source and target distributions through approaches such as adversarial training [15], correlation alignment [16], and adaptive batch normalization [17]. Their application to machinery fault diagnosis has been extensively reviewed and evaluated [9], [27]. Transfer learning from pretrained image models, using time-frequency representations of vibration signals, provides another means of adapting learned features to diagnostic tasks [28].

The effectiveness of these approaches depends on the transfer setting. In many bearing diagnosis studies, the source and target domains correspond to different operating conditions of the same experimental rig. Such evaluations are useful for examining changes in speed or load, but they do not necessarily capture differences in bearing geometry, structural response, and measurement configuration between independent machines. Moreover, classification accuracy is commonly the principal evaluation metric, leaving the reliability of predictive uncertainty under transfer less clearly characterized [9], [27].

The theoretical difficulty of cross-domain learning is reflected in the generalization analysis of Ben-David et al. [29], which relates target-domain error to source-domain error, distributional discrepancy, and the error of a hypothesis suitable for both domains. When source and target machines produce substantially different feature distributions, the discrepancy term becomes important, even if their fault categories are nominally identical. Domain generalization addresses the related problem of learning representations without using target-domain observations. Existing surveys have organized the available approaches [30], while comparative work under controlled model-selection procedures has shown that conventional empirical risk minimization can remain competitive with specialized domain-generalization algorithms [31]. Although these findings originate from broader machine-learning settings, they underline the importance of separating the contribution of a learning algorithm from the influence of the evaluation protocol.

For bearing diagnosis, an additional difficulty arises when the available source machines provide only limited variation in bearing geometry. Under such conditions, a model trained on fixed-frequency or fixed-order features must infer the relationship between geometry and fault signatures from a small number of machine configurations. The experiments in Section 4.2 examine this issue by comparing geometry-anchored features with order-domain features supplemented by geometric parameters. Recent studies have continued to investigate distribution alignment for cross-domain bearing diagnosis, including multi-adversarial adaptation across motor-bearing devices [21] and methods based on improved feature-distribution alignment [22]. These approaches generally rely on target-domain observations during adaptation and assess their performance primarily through diagnostic classification. The setting considered here differs in one important respect: the target machine contributes no labelled data to model training or calibration, and the central question is whether reliable diagnostic predictions can be obtained using information from the available source machines.

sec.title: 2.5. Prediction uncertainty and conformal calibration
sec.p: Accurate fault classification does not necessarily imply reliable predictive confidence. Neural-network classifiers can produce poorly calibrated probabilities [32], and empirical investigations have shown that predictive uncertainty may deteriorate as the difference between training and testing distributions increases [33]. These observations are particularly relevant to cross-machine diagnosis, where changes in geometry and vibration transmission can alter both the feature distribution and the relationship between predicted probabilities and diagnostic correctness.

Conformal prediction provides a model-independent approach to constructing prediction sets with marginal coverage under exchangeability [5], [6]. The informativeness of these sets depends on the choice of nonconformity score and the underlying classifier. Methods for constructing less ambiguous prediction sets [34] and adaptive prediction sets [35] have been developed, while Mondrian conformal procedures use separate calibration thresholds for different classes [36]. These methods address aspects of prediction-set construction, but their conventional coverage guarantees depend on the statistical relationship between calibration and test observations.

Several extensions of conformal prediction are relevant to distribution shift. Weighted conformal prediction accounts for covariate shift through density-ratio information [7], while subsequent work has examined coverage beyond exchangeability [8], label-distribution shift [37], and adaptive inference under changing data distributions [38]. A related line of research uses held-out observations to construct predictive inference procedures. Cross-conformal prediction [11] and jackknife+ methods [12] provide relevant methodological foundations, although their theoretical properties and prediction-set constructions differ. In particular, the general jackknife+ result provides a weaker coverage bound than conventional split conformal prediction, with a bound involving twice the nominal error level [12]. These distinctions are important because excluding complete machines from calibration-model training does not automatically establish the finite-sample guarantees associated with established conformal procedures.

The interpretation of coverage also requires care. The distinction between marginal and conditional coverage is fundamental to distribution-free predictive inference [39]. In cross-machine fault diagnosis, this distinction is particularly relevant because average coverage across machines does not ensure comparable coverage on each individual machine. In cross-machine diagnosis, this distinction separates coverage averaged across machines from coverage obtained on a particular machine. A procedure may achieve the nominal level when averaged over the evaluated machine population while producing substantially lower coverage for equipment with unusual noise, geometry, or vibration characteristics. Conformal risk control extends related ideas toward controlling expected monotone losses [40], providing a statistical perspective for diagnostic decisions in which different classification errors carry different operational costs.

Applications of conformal prediction to machinery diagnosis remain relatively limited. In cross-dataset bearing classification, one study reported empirical coverage near the nominal level even when the underlying classifier performed poorly, but the resulting prediction sets contained more than three of the four available classes at a nominal error level of 0.1 [10]. This illustrates the distinction between statistical coverage and diagnostic informativeness. The reported procedure used labelled target-domain observations for calibration, whereas a newly encountered machine may have no such data available. Conformal anomaly detection has also been investigated for industrial fleet monitoring, including district-heating systems [41], demonstrating the relevance of uncertainty-aware monitoring at the equipment level.

Further developments have examined conditional coverage for specified groups or distribution shifts. Group-aware conformal methods can establish guarantees over predefined collections of groups or structured classes of covariate shifts [23], provided the corresponding assumptions and calibration requirements are satisfied. Other work has proposed diagnostics for identifying vulnerability to distribution shift before model deployment, including investigations involving gradient-boosted classifiers [24]. These studies address important aspects of uncertainty under changing conditions, but their assumptions differ from a setting involving only a small number of source machines and an entirely unseen target machine. In the present study, the calibration units are complete machines, and the available source population contains at most seven machines in each leave-one-machine-out evaluation. This motivates examining machine-level calibration empirically, with particular attention to average coverage, machine-specific coverage, and prediction-set size.

sec.title: 2.6. Unknown-fault detection and cost-sensitive decisions
sec.p: Cross-machine diagnostic reliability also depends on how a classifier responds to faults outside the categories represented during training. Maximum softmax probability provides a conventional baseline for identifying misclassified or out-of-distribution observations [42], while class-conditional Mahalanobis distance offers an alternative based on the distribution of learned features [43]. Selective classification addresses a related decision problem by allowing a model to abstain from prediction and evaluating the relationship between classification accuracy and the proportion of observations receiving a decision [44].

These approaches become more difficult to interpret when an unfamiliar machine introduces distribution shift independently of fault novelty. A low-confidence prediction may arise because the machine differs from those used in training, because the observed fault is unknown, or because the measured signal has poor diagnostic quality. Conversely, an unfamiliar fault may still receive a high-confidence label from one of the known categories. Distinguishing these situations is important in industrial maintenance, where missed faults, unnecessary inspections, and incorrect fault identification have different consequences.

A diagnostic system should therefore be evaluated not only by its classification and detection metrics but also by the operational costs associated with its decisions. Abstention may be preferable when the expected cost of an incorrect diagnosis exceeds the cost of inspection, although this relationship depends on fault prevalence, probability calibration, and the assumed cost matrix. The combined assessment of unknown-fault recognition, selective prediction, and cost-sensitive decisions under machine-level distribution shift provides an additional perspective on the practical reliability of cross-machine diagnostic models.

sec.title: 2.7. Research gaps and hypotheses
sec.p: The preceding review identifies a common methodological issue across the literature: diagnostic accuracy, feature transferability, and prediction uncertainty are often evaluated separately, even though they interact when a model is deployed on previously unseen equipment. The evaluation protocol determines which forms of machine variation are represented in testing; the feature representation determines whether fault information retains consistent meaning across machines; and the calibration procedure determines how prediction uncertainty is translated into diagnostic decisions.

Five research gaps follow from this synthesis. G1 concerns the distinction between evaluation on previously encountered machines and evaluation on genuinely unseen equipment. G2 concerns the loss of machine-independent physical meaning when fault signatures are represented on fixed frequency or order axes. G3 concerns the mismatch between calibration on known machines and prediction under machine-level distribution shift. G4 concerns the need to examine marginal coverage, machine-specific coverage, and prediction-set size together. G5 concerns the limited integration of unknown-fault recognition and operational decision costs into cross-machine diagnostic evaluation. Table 2 summarizes the relationship between the reviewed research directions and these gaps.

sec.p: These gaps provide the basis for seven research hypotheses, summarized in Table 3. The hypotheses were formulated as part of the structured interpretation of the literature and the completed simulation experiments, rather than being registered before the experiments. They are therefore used to organize the evidence and examine the relationships between evaluation protocol, feature representation, calibration, and diagnostic decisions. Their assessment in Section 5.1 follows this exploratory interpretation.

caption.title: Research hypotheses and corresponding experimental analyses

td.p: Random-window and recording-level splits overestimate diagnostic performance on unseen machines when the feature representation retains machine-dependent characteristics.

Geometry-anchored features retain fault-specific physical meaning across machines and provide better diagnostic generalization than fixed-frequency or fixed-order representations. With limited source machines, appending geometric parameters to conventional features does not provide an equivalent representation.

Calibration using observations from previously encountered machines produces insufficient coverage under machine shift, whereas calibration based on nested machine holdouts improves average coverage on unseen machines.

Prediction-set coverage alone does not establish diagnostic informativeness. Small and informative prediction sets depend on feature representations that preserve fault discrimination across machines.

Marginal coverage averaged across machines does not ensure nominal coverage for each machine. Conservative machine-level thresholds improve coverage on poorly represented machines at the cost of larger prediction sets.

Under machine-level distribution shift and with a limited number of source machines, density-ratio weighting, conventional open-set detection, and cost-sensitive abstention do not consistently improve diagnostic reliability.

The relative performance of geometry-anchored features and machine-level calibration remains consistent across the examined model variations and moderate departures from nominal kinematic assumptions, although individual machines may experience reduced reliability.

sec.p: Taken together, these hypotheses establish a common basis for examining the interaction between evaluation protocol, feature representation, and uncertainty calibration. H1 and H2 address the sources of apparent diagnostic generalization and the role of physically indexed fault information. H3–H5 concern the relationship between machine-level calibration, prediction-set informativeness, and coverage variation across machines. H6 extends the evaluation to unknown faults and operational decisions, while H7 examines the stability of the principal findings under changes in signal characteristics and classification models. The controlled simulation described in Section 3 was designed to provide comparable evidence across these aspects of cross-machine diagnosis, with the corresponding experimental results presented in Section 4.

sec.title: 3. Hybrid study design and methods
sec.p: The study employed a controlled simulation framework to investigate the relationship between feature representation, machine-level distribution shift, and uncertainty calibration in cross-machine bearing fault diagnosis. Public bearing datasets provide valuable experimental evidence, but relatively few contain multiple independent machines with fully documented bearing geometries. Moreover, differences in fault characteristics, sensor configurations, and structural transmission paths often occur simultaneously, making their individual effects difficult to distinguish. Controlled simulation allowed these factors to be examined under known ground-truth conditions while maintaining consistent evaluation procedures across diagnostic methods.

The methodological framework comprised leave-one-machine-out evaluation, signal processing and feature construction, conformal calibration, robustness and decision analyses, and analytical examination of fault-frequency ambiguity. Sections 3.1–3.8 describe the simulation, feature extraction, calibration, and evaluation procedures, while Section 3.9 presents the deterministic analysis of fault-frequency ambiguity across the simulated machines. The findings are synthesized in Section 5, followed by a discussion of their implications for industrial condition monitoring in Section 6.

All characteristic orders were expressed relative to shaft rotational frequency. Inner-race fault signals were amplitude-modulated at shaft frequency, whereas ball-fault signals were modulated at the cage frequency. Mechanical looseness, which served as the unknown fault condition, was represented by excitation components at 0.5 and 1 shaft orders.

Timing jitter of 1% was introduced to approximate rolling-element slip. Fault severity was sampled from a log-uniform distribution at the recording level, while rotational speed, noise amplitude, and interference characteristics varied between recordings. Each machine had its own bearing geometry, shaft speed, sampling rate, structural resonance, noise level, signal gain, and interference rate. Shaft frequencies ranged from 20 to 45 Hz, sampling frequencies from 12 to 25.6 kHz, and structural resonances from 2.5 to 7 kHz. The individual machine parameters are provided in Appendix A.

Eight machines, designated M1–M8, were simulated under five conditions: normal operation, inner-race fault, outer-race fault, ball fault, and mechanical looseness. Four recordings were generated for each machine–condition combination, with twelve non-overlapping windows per recording. This produced 48 windows per machine and condition, 240 windows per machine, and 1,920 windows per random seed. Windows belonging to the same recording shared their speed, noise characteristics, interference amplitude, and fault severity.

The simulated configurations also included overlapping characteristic fault orders between different machines. For example, the inner-race fault order of M5 was close to the outer-race fault order of M6. Such overlap introduces ambiguity when fault signatures are represented on a common order axis without accounting for bearing geometry. Figure 2 illustrates the characteristic fault orders of the eight machines, while Table 4 summarizes the simulation design.

sec.title: 3.3. Signal processing and feature representations
sec.p: All feature representations were extracted from a common signal-processing pipeline to ensure that differences in diagnostic performance could be attributed primarily to feature construction rather than to separate preprocessing procedures.

For each vibration window, the resonance band was selected from fourteen candidate bands according to maximum envelope kurtosis. The Hilbert transform was then used to obtain the signal envelope, from which the envelope spectrum was calculated. Spectral amplitudes were normalized by the median spectral level between 3 and 800 Hz, yielding features expressed relative to the background spectral floor.
Three representations were constructed.

Frequency-domain representation. The envelope spectrum between 0 and 500 Hz was divided into fifty frequency intervals of 10 Hz. The maximum amplitude within each interval was retained and logarithmically transformed. This representation preserved spectral information at fixed physical frequencies without explicitly incorporating shaft speed or bearing geometry.

Order-domain representation. Spectral frequencies were normalized by the estimated shaft rotational frequency. Features were extracted between 0.3 and 10 shaft orders at intervals of 0.1, producing 98 features. The shaft-frequency estimate included a random error of 0.3%. This representation accounted for differences in rotational speed while retaining a common order axis across machines.

Geometry-anchored kinematic representation. Twenty features were calculated using characteristic fault orders derived from each machine’s bearing geometry and rotational speed. Spectral amplitudes were extracted within a
± 3
tolerance band around the calculated fault orders. Twelve features represented the first three harmonics of FTF, twice the ball-spin frequency, BPFO, and BPFI. Four additional features described shaft-order and cage-related sidebands around BPFI and twice the ball-spin frequency. Three features represented amplitudes at 0.5, 1, and 2 shaft orders, and the remaining feature was envelope kurtosis.

The central distinction between these representations concerns the physical meaning of their feature coordinates. Frequency-domain features were indexed by fixed frequencies, and order-domain features by normalized frequencies. In contrast, geometry-anchored features were indexed by characteristic fault mechanisms, allowing the same feature position to refer to the same physical quantity across different bearing configurations.

The kinematic representation required bearing geometry and shaft speed to be available for each machine. These requirements were retained throughout the evaluation, and their influence was examined through controlled geometry and speed perturbations in Section 4.6. Their practical implications for industrial condition monitoring are discussed in Section 6.3.

sec.title: 3.4. Classification models and baselines
sec.p: The principal diagnostic classifier was a histogram-based gradient-boosting model implemented using scikit-learn [45]. The model used 60 boosting iterations, a maximum tree depth of 3, a learning rate of 0.1, and an L2 regularization parameter of 1. The same configuration was applied to the three feature representations without representation-specific hyperparameter optimization.
Several additional configurations were evaluated to distinguish the influence of feature representation from that of the classifier or adaptation procedure.

First, per-machine feature standardization was applied using unlabelled target-machine statistics, following an adaptive-normalization strategy related to Adaptive Batch Normalization (AdaBN) [17]. This configuration examined whether adjusting feature distributions using target-machine observations could improve cross-machine diagnosis.

Second, a multilayer perceptron with one hidden layer containing 64 units was evaluated on the same feature representations. This provided a neural-network comparison with the principal gradient-boosting classifier.

Third, the order-domain representation was supplemented with a vector of bearing geometry parameters. This configuration, denoted order+geo, examined whether a classifier trained on a limited number of machines could learn the relationship between geometric parameters and characteristic fault orders without explicitly constructing geometry-anchored features.
The comparisons were designed to isolate the effects of feature construction, target-machine normalization, and classifier selection while maintaining consistent machine-level evaluation conditions.

sec.title: 3.6. Unknown-fault detection and decision analysis
sec.p: The evaluation was extended beyond closed-set fault classification to examine unknown-fault recognition and the consequences of diagnostic decisions. Mechanical looseness served as the unknown condition because it was excluded from the four-class training label space.

For conformal prediction, a window was flagged as potentially unknown when its prediction set was empty. This rule was evaluated together with two conventional novelty scores: maximum predicted class probability and minimum class-conditional Mahalanobis distance. The Mahalanobis calculation used a shared covariance matrix estimated using the Ledoit–Wolf procedure, with and without per-machine feature standardization. Detection performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC).

A cost-sensitive decision analysis was also conducted to examine the relationship between diagnostic predictions and maintenance actions. The available actions consisted of assigning one of the four known fault labels or abstaining from classification and referring the observation for inspection.

The decision costs were specified as follows: correct classification, 0; classifying a fault as normal, 10; falsely identifying a fault in a normal window, 1; assigning an incorrect fault category, 2; and abstaining for inspection, 0.3.

Four decision policies were compared: direct classification using the highest predicted probability, a Bayes decision rule minimizing expected cost under the estimated class probabilities, and two singleton-set decision rules using LMO-CP and naive conformal thresholds, respectively. Under the singleton-set policies, a class label was assigned only when the prediction set contained exactly one class; otherwise, the system abstained.

A policy that always referred observations for inspection was included as a reference, with a constant cost of 0.3 per window. This comparison allowed the decision analysis to distinguish improvements in classification performance from reductions in expected operational cost under the specified cost assumptions.

sec.title: 3.7. Machine-level evaluation protocol
sec.p: Generalization was evaluated using leave-one-machine-out testing. Each of the eight simulated machines was excluded from model development in turn and used as the target machine, while the remaining seven machines provided the source observations.

Classification accuracy, macro-F1, expected calibration error, and conformal coverage were calculated using the known-class windows of the held-out machine. Unknown-fault windows were included in the open-set and relevant decision analyses. The principal results were summarized as the mean and standard deviation, across five random seeds, of the average performance over the eight held-out machines.

To characterize differences between machines, the worst-machine coverage was calculated as the lowest coverage among the eight machines for each seed and then averaged across seeds. The proportion of machine–seed cases achieving coverage within 0.05 below the nominal target was also reported. For a nominal miscoverage level
α
, the corresponding threshold was the nominal coverage minus 0.05.
With eight machines and five seeds, the principal experiment contained forty machine–seed evaluation cases.

A separate leakage audit compared three evaluation protocols: random 80:20 window splitting, 80:20 recording-level splitting, and leave-one-machine-out testing. This comparison examined how the unit of data separation influenced apparent diagnostic performance.

Table 5 summarizes the assignment of observations to training, calibration, and testing under the four conformal procedures. Under naive calibration, windows from the same recording could be shared between training and calibration. Recording-level separation removed this overlap, while LMO-CP excluded the complete calibration machine from the corresponding nested model. The target machine was excluded from supervised training and calibration in all procedures. Unlabelled target observations were used only in the weighted calibration and per-machine standardization configurations.

sec.title: 3.8. Statistical, ablation, and robustness analyses
sec.p: Additional analyses were conducted to examine the consistency of the principal findings across machines, identify the contribution of individual kinematic feature groups, and assess the sensitivity of diagnostic performance and conformal calibration to changes in signal characteristics and classifier selection. Six complementary analyses were performed within the experimental framework described above.

Statistical comparisons. Paired differences between methods were calculated across 40 machine–seed evaluation cases obtained from eight held-out machines and five random seeds. Bootstrap confidence intervals were estimated using 10,000 resamples of these cases and describe variability within the simulated evaluation design. Because repeated evaluations of the same machine were not independent machine-level observations, statistical significance was assessed separately using an exact two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test on the eight machine-level mean differences. sec.title: 3.9. Structural audit of fault-line ambiguity
sec.p: The final analysis examined the extent to which characteristic bearing fault frequencies could be distinguished across machines using fixed frequency and order coordinates. Unlike the preceding simulation experiments, this assessment was deterministic and used only the machine parameters listed in Table A1. No random signal generation or additional classifier training was required to calculate the fault-line collisions.

Three characteristic fault orders were considered for each machine: BPFO for outer-race faults, BPFI for inner-race faults, and twice the ball-spin frequency (2
×
BSF) for ball faults. The orders were calculated using the bearing kinematic relationships described in Section 3.2, producing 24 fault-defining lines across the eight simulated machines.

A cross-machine collision was identified when a characteristic fault order lay within 3% of the order associated with a different fault on another machine. The relative tolerance corresponded to the search band used by the geometry-anchored feature extractor. Collisions between different fault categories within the same machine were treated separately and were not included in the cross-machine collision count.

For the frequency-domain representation, a collision was identified when characteristic fault frequencies associated with different faults on different machines occupied the same 10 Hz interval used by the fixed-frequency features. These two criteria allowed structural ambiguity to be examined independently on the normalized order axis and the physical frequency axis.

To assess the diagnostic consequences of this ambiguity, an idealized leave-one-machine-out nearest-line classifier was evaluated. Each machine was excluded in turn, and its characteristic fault lines were compared with those of the remaining seven machines. For each fault line of the held-out machine, the predicted category was assigned according to the nearest characteristic line among the source machines, with distance measured on a logarithmic axis.

The classifier operated on three fault categories, giving a chance-level accuracy of 1/3. It was evaluated without noise, interference, or amplitude variation, so its results represented the structural discriminative information available from fault-line positions rather than the performance of a complete vibration-based diagnostic model.

The audit also distinguished between two properties of fixed-axis representations. Cross-fault collision described cases in which similar frequency or order coordinates corresponded to different fault mechanisms on different machines. Same-fault agreement described cases in which the characteristic lines of the same fault occurred at similar coordinates across different machines. The former measures ambiguity in fault identification, whereas the latter indicates the consistency of fault-related information available to a classifier operating on a fixed axis.

The results of this analysis are presented in Section 4.15, with the individual fault-line collisions reported in Appendix C. Together with the classification experiments, the audit provides a physical basis for interpreting the differences between fixed-axis and geometry-anchored feature representations under machine-level distribution shift.

sec.title: 4.4. Machine-specific variation in prediction-set coverage
sec.p: The results in Section 4.3 establish the average empirical performance of the calibration procedures, but they do not describe the reliability experienced by every individual machine. Marginal coverage concerns observations averaged over the evaluated machine population, whereas machine-specific coverage is calculated for a particular machine. These quantities are distinct. The general limitations of distribution-free conditional coverage [39] also motivate distinguishing average coverage from coverage conditional on a particular machine.

With kinematic features and LMO-CP, mean coverage across individual machines ranged from 0.777 for M4 to 0.994 for M3 (Table 9 and Figure 5). The average of the lowest machine coverage within each seed was 0.751, showing that the minimum within a seed could fall below the minimum of the machine-level means reported in Table 9. Nevertheless, 80% of the forty machine–seed cases achieved coverage of at least 0.85, compared with 68% under naive calibration.

Machine-specific coverage under naive and LMO-CP calibration at 90% nominal coverage

sec.p: The largest departure from nominal coverage occurred on M4, which combined the lowest signal gain with the highest noise level among the simulated machines. Its kinematic LMO-CP coverage was 0.777, compared with 0.758 under naive calibration. M2 had the second-lowest kinematic LMO-CP coverage at 0.862. Its inner-race and ball-fault characteristic orders coincided at 4.8 shaft orders, creating an additional source of spectral ambiguity examined in Section 4.15. In contrast, M3 achieved coverage of 0.994, while M5 and M6 reached 0.951 and 0.954, respectively.

Seven of the eight machines achieved mean kinematic LMO-CP coverage of at least 0.85. The difference between M4 and M3 nevertheless demonstrates that average coverage close to the nominal level can coexist with substantial variation across machine configurations. The results therefore support evaluating machine-specific coverage alongside the overall average, particularly when the target machine differs markedly from the source population.

sec.title: 4.7. Sensitivity to signal-to-noise ratio
sec.p: The preceding analysis examined errors in the physical parameters used for feature extraction. A complementary experiment investigated how diagnostic performance changed when fault-related vibration components became more or less distinguishable from background noise. Signal difficulty was adjusted by rescaling fault severity, while the remaining simulation procedures were retained. Two additional random seeds were used for each modified signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) condition, and the five-seed reference results were included for comparison.

The geometry-anchored representation maintained the highest classification accuracy across all three SNR conditions. At high SNR, it achieved an accuracy of 0.95, compared with 0.65 for frequency-domain features and 0.62 for order-domain features. Under the reference condition, the corresponding accuracies were approximately 0.91, 0.58, and 0.57. At low SNR, accuracy decreased to 0.71 for geometry-anchored features, while the frequency-domain and order-domain representations reached 0.42 and 0.41, respectively. As summarized in Table 11, the separation between the representations persisted even when the fault-related signal components became substantially weaker.

caption.title: Effects of signal-to-noise ratio on diagnostic performance

sec.p: The calibration results showed that decreasing SNR affected prediction-set informativeness more strongly than average coverage. With geometry-anchored features, LMO-CP achieved coverage of approximately 0.91, 0.90, and 0.90 under high, reference, and low SNR conditions, respectively. Mean prediction-set size, however, increased from 0.93 classes at high SNR to 0.99 under the reference condition and 1.89 at low SNR. The naive calibration procedure also produced larger sets as signal quality decreased, but its average coverage remained below the nominal level.

For order-domain features, LMO-CP maintained coverage between 0.91 and 0.94 across the three SNR conditions, despite substantially lower classification accuracy. These results reinforce the distinction between obtaining nominal empirical coverage and producing diagnostically informative prediction sets. When fault signatures became difficult to distinguish, the calibration procedure maintained coverage primarily by admitting more candidate classes.

sec.title: 4.8. Unknown-fault detection, selective classification, and cost-sensitive decisions
sec.p: The previous experiments concerned faults represented in the training data. Industrial diagnostic systems must also respond to observations that do not correspond to any known fault category. Mechanical looseness was therefore introduced as an unknown condition, and its detection was examined alongside selective classification and cost-sensitive decision-making.

Selective classification produced the expected relationship between the fraction of windows receiving a prediction and the accuracy of those predictions. As the model abstained from an increasing proportion of low-confidence observations, accuracy on the remaining windows improved. This effect was most apparent for geometry-anchored features, as illustrated in Figure 8. However, the ability to identify misclassified known faults did not translate directly into reliable recognition of the unknown looseness condition.

The relative performance of these decision policies depended on the assumed costs. Under the Bayes rule, abstention was selected whenever the lowest expected cost of assigning a class exceeded the inspection cost. Reducing the inspection cost or increasing the penalty for missed faults therefore favored more frequent abstention, bringing the resulting cost closer to that of inspecting every observation. For geometry-anchored features, the expected calibration error was 0.052 in the reference experiment. Even with this level of probability calibration, the difference between the Bayes decision cost and the constant inspection cost was only 0.011, considerably smaller than the observed variation across machine–seed evaluations. The results therefore showed that improved classification accuracy and conformal coverage did not automatically translate into lower operational cost under the selected decision assumptions.

The pronounced contribution of BPFO harmonics is consistent with the signal-generation mechanism. In the reference simulator, outer-race faults were represented primarily by impulses at the characteristic BPFO order and its harmonics, without additional modulation sidebands. sec.title: 4.11. Class-specific diagnostic performance and unknown-fault classification
sec.p: The aggregate accuracy results were examined further to determine how diagnostic errors were distributed among individual fault categories. Figure 10 presents the row-normalized confusion matrices obtained from the held-out machines, including the predicted labels assigned to the unknown mechanical-looseness condition.

caption.title: Row-normalized confusion matrices for held-out machines, including the unknown looseness condition

sec.p: Geometry-anchored features achieved recall values of 0.93 for normal operation, 0.91 for inner-race faults, 0.94 for outer-race faults, and 0.85 for ball faults. Ball faults were the most difficult known condition, with approximately 13% of their windows classified as normal. Nevertheless, the representation maintained relatively balanced recognition across the four known classes.

The fixed-axis representations exhibited more pronounced class-dependent errors. With order-domain features, outer-race faults were correctly identified in only 17% of windows, while 63% were classified as normal. Ball-fault recall was 0.48. The frequency-domain representation produced recall values of approximately 0.51, 0.50, and 0.43 for inner-race, outer-race, and ball faults, respectively. These patterns are consistent with the ambiguity introduced when characteristic fault frequencies occupy different spectral positions across bearing configurations, or when similar positions correspond to different fault mechanisms.

The unknown mechanical-looseness condition revealed a separate difficulty. Even with geometry-anchored features, approximately 70% of unknown-fault windows were classified as normal. The remaining observations were assigned to inner-race faults (20%), outer-race faults (3%), and ball faults (7%). Because looseness was excluded from the training label space, these predictions reflected the tendency of the closed-set classifier to assign unfamiliar observations to the available categories.

The confusion analysis therefore distinguishes two aspects of diagnostic performance. Geometry-anchored features improved discrimination among the fault classes represented during training, but this improvement did not establish reliable recognition of an unknown fault. The novelty-detection results in Section 4.8 further showed that conventional confidence-based and conformal empty-set rules did not consistently resolve this distinction under the simulated machine shifts.

sec.title: 4.12. Class-conditional, conservative, and adaptive conformal calibration
sec.p: The preceding calibration results were based primarily on coverage averaged across machines and fault classes. To examine whether alternative calibration procedures could improve reliability for individual classes or atypical machines, pooled LMO-CP was compared with class-conditional, conservative, and adaptive-score variants. The results are summarized in Table 15 and Figure 11.

sec.title: 4.13. Robustness under kinematic model mismatch
sec.p: The reference simulation generated fault-related impulses at characteristic orders calculated directly from the same bearing kinematic relationships used for feature extraction. To examine how departures from these relationships affected diagnostic performance, the stress test introduced additional slip, recording-level fault-order perturbations, and within-window speed variation, as described in Section 3.8. Table 16 compares diagnostic accuracy, conformal coverage, prediction-set size, and worst-machine coverage before and after the kinematic model-mismatch stress test.

caption.title: Diagnostic performance under kinematic model mismatch (three seeds)

sec.p: Under the reference conditions for the same three seeds, geometry-anchored features achieved an accuracy of approximately 0.90. Accuracy decreased to 0.84 under the stress-test conditions. Despite this reduction, the geometry-anchored representation remained more accurate than both fixed-axis alternatives, which achieved 0.62 for order-domain features and 0.56 for frequency-domain features. The corresponding changes in the fixed-axis representations were comparatively small relative to their seed-to-seed variation.

The effect on conformal calibration was more complex. With geometry-anchored features, LMO-CP maintained average coverage close to 0.90, decreasing from approximately 0.91 under the reference conditions to 0.90 under model mismatch. Mean prediction-set size increased from 1.01 to 1.22 classes, indicating that the additional signal variation required less selective prediction sets to maintain aggregate coverage.

Machine-specific reliability was more strongly affected. Worst-machine coverage decreased from 0.77 to 0.61, while the proportion of machine–seed cases achieving coverage within 0.05 of the nominal target decreased from 83% to 79%. Thus, the average coverage remained close to nominal even though the least well-covered machine experienced a substantial deterioration.

The stress-test results show that geometry-anchored features retained a classification advantage under the specified departures from nominal bearing kinematics. They also establish that average conformal coverage and worst-machine coverage can respond differently to model mismatch. The experiment retained the underlying impulse-response structure of the reference simulator, so the observed robustness characterizes the evaluated perturbations rather than the full range of vibration conditions encountered in physical machinery.

sec.title: 4.14. Dependence on classifier selection
sec.p: The reference experiments used histogram-based gradient boosting as the principal diagnostic classifier. To determine whether the observed differences between feature representations were specific to this model, the evaluation was repeated using standardized logistic regression and a random forest. Both classifiers were assessed using the same three random seeds and leave-one-machine-out protocol.

As shown in Table 17, geometry-anchored features achieved an accuracy of approximately 0.90 with both logistic regression and random forest. By comparison, order-domain features achieved 0.50 with logistic regression and 0.59 with random forest. The classification advantage of physically indexed fault features therefore persisted across the evaluated learning algorithms, indicating that the observed improvement was not restricted to the gradient-boosting classifier.

caption.title: Diagnostic performance across different classifiers (three seeds)

sec.p: The conformal results followed a similar pattern. For geometry-anchored features, naive calibration produced coverage of 0.88 with logistic regression and 0.89 with random forest. LMO-CP increased coverage to approximately 0.90 for both classifiers, while mean prediction-set size remained close to one class. With order-domain features, naive coverage was 0.73 and 0.65 for logistic regression and random forest, respectively. LMO-CP increased coverage to 0.92 and 0.90, but the resulting prediction sets contained approximately three classes on average.

The consistency of these results across gradient boosting, logistic regression, and random forest indicates that the principal differences between the representations arose from how fault-related information was encoded rather than from the choice of classifier alone. Machine-level calibration also produced similar changes in empirical coverage across the evaluated models. However, the diagnostic informativeness of the calibrated prediction sets remained strongly dependent on the feature representation. These findings support the use of physically indexed fault features as a common input to different classification models within the simulated cross-machine setting.

sec.title: 4.15. Structural ambiguity of fixed frequency and order representations
sec.p: The preceding experiments demonstrated that geometry-anchored features provided more consistent cross-machine diagnostic performance than fixed-frequency and order-domain representations. The structural fault-line audit described in Section 3.9 was conducted to examine the physical basis of these differences. Unlike the classification experiments, this analysis used only the bearing parameters listed in Table A1 and did not involve simulated noise, signal amplitudes, or trained diagnostic models.

Across the eight simulated machines, 24 characteristic fault lines were examined, comprising BPFO, BPFI, and twice the ball-spin frequency for each machine. On the order axis, 13 of these 24 lines (54%) lay within 3% of a characteristic line associated with a different fault on another machine, producing eight distinct cross-fault collision pairs (16 directed collision records). Increasing the tolerance to 5% raised the number of affected lines to 16 (67%). A comparable pattern was observed in the frequency domain, where 13 of the 24 lines occupied the same 10 Hz interval as a different-fault line from another machine.

Agreement between machines for the same fault was much less frequent. Among 168 directed same-fault, cross-machine line comparisons, only eight (4.8%) agreed within 3% on the order axis, while twelve (7.1%) occupied the same 10 Hz interval on the frequency axis. These results indicate that fixed spectral coordinates contained both substantial cross-fault ambiguity and limited consistency for the same fault mechanism across machines. The collision statistics are summarized in Table 18, while the machine-specific collision records, including the corresponding fault types, order values, and cross-machine matches, are provided in Table C1 (Appendix C).

sec.p: The diagnostic consequences of this ambiguity were examined using the noise-free nearest-line classifier. Under leave-one-machine-out evaluation, the classifier achieved an accuracy of 0.333 on the order axis, corresponding to the chance level for three fault categories. The frequency-domain representation achieved 0.583, with machines M1, M3, and M5 classified correctly across all three fault lines. Although the frequency axis performed better in this particular configuration, neither fixed-axis representation consistently preserved the relationship between fault-line position and fault category across the eight machines.

The geometry-anchored representation provided a contrasting reference. Because its features were indexed by fault-specific characteristic orders calculated from each machine’s geometry, the corresponding idealized identification accuracy was 1.0 by construction, as illustrated in Figure 12. This value represents the structural correspondence between feature coordinates and fault mechanisms, rather than the accuracy of a trained classifier on vibration signals.

sec.p: The direction of these analytical results was consistent with the leave-one-machine-out classification results in Table 7, where order-domain and frequency-domain features achieved accuracies of 0.575 and 0.585, respectively. The numerical values are not directly comparable, however, because the trained classifiers also processed normal-condition windows, spectral amplitudes, noise, and interference components. The structural audit isolates the ambiguity associated with fault-line positions, whereas the classification experiments measure the combined effect of the complete feature representations.

A further example occurred in machine M2, where the inner-race and ball-fault characteristic lines coincided at 4.8 shaft orders. In this configuration, the fundamental fault order alone could not distinguish the two mechanisms, making additional spectral information, including modulation sidebands, important for discrimination. M2 also exhibited the second-lowest geometry-anchored LMO-CP coverage, at 0.862, compared with 0.777 for M4 (Table 9). The coincident characteristic lines provide a possible physical explanation for the reduced coverage on M2, although the present audit does not isolate their contribution from other machine-dependent factors.

Taken together, the collision statistics and nearest-line analysis explain why a common frequency or order axis can produce conflicting fault information when bearing geometry changes. Geometry-anchored features address this structural difficulty by extracting spectral information at fault-specific locations determined for each machine. The analysis therefore provides a physical interpretation of the classification and calibration results obtained under machine-level distribution shift.

5.1. Assessment of the research hypotheses
sec.p: The seven hypotheses developed from the literature synthesis were assessed against the controlled simulation results. The assessment considered the direction and consistency of the experimental findings, the paired statistical comparisons, and the analytical investigations reported in Section 4. A hypothesis was classified as supported when the simulated evidence consistently agreed with its proposed relationship, and as partly supported when the results depended on the feature representation, calibration procedure, or experimental condition.

As explained in Section 2.7, the hypotheses were formalized after the initial experiments had been completed. Their assessment therefore provides a structured interpretation of the simulation findings rather than a set of preregistered confirmatory tests. sec.p: The hypothesis assessments reveal two closely connected findings. First, the choice of feature representation determined whether fault-related information remained discriminative when the target machine differed from those used for training. Second, the calibration procedure determined how uncertainty was expressed under that shift, but it could not compensate for a representation that failed to distinguish fault categories. This distinction explains why machine-level calibration produced prediction sets close to nominal coverage for all three representations, whereas only the geometry-anchored representation maintained small sets.

The results also distinguish aggregate calibration from reliability on individual machines. Although pooled LMO-CP achieved average coverage close to the nominal level, the worst-machine results varied substantially. Conservative calibration reduced this variation at the cost of larger prediction sets. These observations motivate the analytical examination of machine-level coverage in the following section.

This argument concerns the relative ranks of population-level machine quantiles. It does not establish a finite-sample coverage theorem for the implemented LMO-CP procedure, in which each machine contributes a finite collection of potentially dependent windows and the final classifier differs from the nested calibration models. The pooled calibration threshold also differs from the conservative threshold because it combines machine-level scores rather than selecting the largest machine-specific quantile.

The empirical results were consistent with the direction of the rank argument. With geometry-anchored features, LMO-max increased worst-machine coverage from 0.751 to 0.866, while mean prediction-set size increased from 0.99 to 1.50 classes (Table 15). In addition, 95% of machine–seed cases achieved coverage of at least 0.85. This empirical criterion differs from the nominal 0.90 coverage level considered in Proposition 1, so the result should not be interpreted as a direct verification of the proposition. Rather, the analysis explains why conservative machine-level calibration can improve coverage across heterogeneous machines and why the number of independent source machines matters when interpreting reliability at the machine level.

sec.title: 5.3. Relationship to previous research
sec.p: The findings can be understood in relation to several established results in cross-domain diagnosis and predictive uncertainty. The substantial reduction in fixed-axis classification accuracy under machine holdout resembles the cross-dataset performance deterioration reported for bearing diagnosis between CWRU and SEU [10]. Similarly, the loss of empirical coverage under machine shift is consistent with broader observations that predictive uncertainty becomes less reliable as the test distribution departs from the training distribution [33].

The behavior of weighted conformal calibration provides a further connection to domain-adaptation theory. In the experiments, the domain classifier distinguished source and target machines with high accuracy, leaving normalized effective sample sizes of only 4%–14% after weighting. This behavior is consistent with the difficulty of transferring predictions when source and target feature distributions differ substantially, as reflected in theoretical analyses of domain adaptation [29]. The observed variation in coverage between individual machines is also consistent with the limitations of distribution-free conditional coverage [39].

The present study extends these observations by examining feature representation and calibration within the same machine-level evaluation framework. Geometry-anchored features preserved the physical association between feature coordinates and bearing fault mechanisms, while nested machine holdouts produced calibration scores under a transfer setting closer to the target evaluation. Their joint assessment showed that improved empirical coverage was most informative when the representation also maintained diagnostic discrimination. The resulting distinction between coverage and prediction-set size provides a basis for evaluating uncertainty-aware diagnosis beyond classification accuracy alone.

sec.p: The methodological and experimental findings were consolidated into a reporting checklist for studies evaluating bearing diagnosis on previously unseen machines. The twelve reporting requirements listed in Table 20 address the principal sources of variation identified in the review and examined in the controlled experiments. Its purpose is to make the evaluation setting, calibration assumptions, and operational interpretation of diagnostic predictions explicit.
