They also encourage separate reporting of classification accuracy, prediction-set coverage, and the diagnostic information retained within the prediction sets. For industrial applications, this distinction is particularly important because a statistically well-covered prediction set may still contain too many candidate faults to support a specific maintenance decision.

sec.title: 6.1. Principal findings
sec.p: The experiments revealed a clear distinction between diagnostic discrimination and prediction reliability. Geometry-anchored features reduced the dependence of fault classification on machine-specific spectral coordinates, whereas machine-level calibration addressed the uncertainty associated with transferring predictions to unseen machines. The evaluation protocol provided a separate means of determining whether these effects persisted when complete machines were excluded from model development. Together, these three elements defined the experimental assessment of cross-machine diagnostic reliability.

The difference between random splitting and machine-level holdout was particularly pronounced for fixed-axis representations. Random window splitting overestimated diagnostic accuracy by as much as 0.29, while recording-level separation did not fully expose the deterioration associated with an unseen machine. Geometry-anchored features, by contrast, maintained substantially higher accuracy across the evaluation protocols. The ablation experiments in Section 4.10 showed that the characteristic fault-order amplitudes accounted for much of this advantage, while the structural audit in Section 4.15 identified the ambiguity introduced when similar frequency or order coordinates corresponded to different fault mechanisms across machines.

The calibration results revealed a complementary relationship. For machine-dependent representations, calibration using observations from previously encountered machines produced prediction sets with coverage below the nominal target. LMO-CP improved average empirical coverage by generating calibration scores from models that had not encountered the corresponding calibration machine. However, the improvement in coverage did not necessarily produce informative diagnostic predictions. With fixed-axis representations, the calibrated sets contained nearly three of the four known classes on average, whereas geometry-anchored features produced sets containing approximately one class. This distinction indicates that the effectiveness of uncertainty calibration depends partly on whether the underlying representation preserves fault discrimination across machines.

Machine-specific coverage introduced a further consideration. Although pooled LMO-CP achieved average coverage close to the nominal level, individual machines exhibited substantial differences. Conservative calibration increased worst-machine coverage but required larger prediction sets. The analytical argument in Section 5.2 also demonstrated how the number of independent source machines constrains machine-level coverage statements under idealized exchangeability assumptions. These findings distinguish empirical average coverage from reliability on a particular machine and show why both quantities should be reported when assessing cross-machine diagnosis.

The unknown-fault and decision analyses identified a separate challenge. Approximately 70% of the mechanical-looseness windows were classified as normal, despite the improved discrimination of known faults achieved by geometry-anchored features. The evaluated novelty-detection and abstention procedures did not consistently reduce operational costs under the specified decision assumptions. Thus, reliable classification among known fault categories and recognition of previously unseen fault mechanisms represent distinct requirements of an industrial diagnostic system.

The combined findings indicate that geometry-anchored features and machine-level conformal calibration address complementary aspects of cross-machine diagnosis. Physically indexed features support fault discrimination across bearing configurations, while machine-level calibration provides an empirical means of assessing prediction-set coverage under machine shift without labelled target-machine observations. Their joint evaluation offers a more complete account of diagnostic performance than classification accuracy alone. sec.title: 6.2. Implications for industrial condition monitoring
sec.p: The results have several implications for the development and evaluation of intelligent bearing-monitoring systems. The first concerns the selection of evaluation data. When a diagnostic model is intended for equipment not represented during training, random window splitting or recording-level separation alone does not establish cross-machine generalization. Machine-level holdout provides a more appropriate assessment because it separates the equipment used for model development from that used for testing. This distinction is particularly important when bearing geometry, sensor placement, and structural vibration transmission differ between source and target machines.

The second implication concerns feature construction. Where bearing geometry and rotational speed are available, characteristic fault frequencies can be incorporated directly into the representation rather than leaving their relationship to fault categories for a classifier to infer from a limited number of machines. The sensitivity experiments in Section 4.6 showed that the accuracy of this representation depended on the quality of the geometric and speed information supplied to the feature extractor. Consequently, the availability and precision of these parameters should be considered part of the diagnostic system specification.

The third implication concerns the interpretation of uncertainty. Prediction-set coverage should be reported together with set size and machine-specific performance. A set containing several fault classes may satisfy an aggregate coverage target while providing limited guidance for maintenance decisions. Similarly, average coverage close to the nominal level may conceal substantially lower coverage on individual machines. The choice between pooled and conservative machine-level calibration should therefore reflect the relative importance of diagnostic specificity and coverage on atypical equipment. In applications where missed faults carry substantial consequences, a conservative threshold may be preferable, provided that the resulting increase in prediction-set size is acceptable.

sec.title: 6.3. Applicability to industrial bearing systems
sec.p: The geometry-anchored representation requires information about bearing geometry and shaft rotational speed. The geometric parameters include the number of rolling elements, the ratio of rolling-element diameter to pitch diameter, and the contact angle. In industrial equipment, these parameters may be obtained from bearing designations, manufacturer catalogues, maintenance records, or machine drawings. Once the bearing configuration is identified, the characteristic fault orders can be calculated using the kinematic relationships described in Section 3.2 [13].

Rotational speed may be measured using a tachometer or keyphasor, obtained from the operating information of a variable-speed drive, or estimated from motor operating parameters. Where direct measurements are unavailable, shaft speed may also be estimated from the vibration spectrum. The accuracy of these inputs becomes particularly important when bearings have been replaced without updated maintenance records, when the installed bearing type is unknown, or when mechanical transmission elements separate the motor from the monitored bearing.

The parameter-sensitivity experiments provide an indication of the required precision. A 1% speed error produced an accuracy of 0.867, close to the 0.870 obtained with exact inputs, whereas a 2% error reduced accuracy to 0.834. Errors in the bearing diameter ratio had a greater effect: accuracy decreased to 0.823 with a 3% error and to 0.807 with a 6% error. The largest geometric perturbation, combining a 10% diameter-ratio error with a $5^{\circ}$ contact-angle error, reduced accuracy to 0.762. Across these conditions, average LMO-CP coverage remained close to 0.90, while mean prediction-set size increased from 1.10 to as much as 1.61 classes (Table 10).

These results indicate that geometry-anchored diagnosis is most suitable when the installed bearing can be identified, its geometric parameters are documented, and shaft speed is measured or estimated with sufficient precision. The approach also requires vibration measurements in which characteristic bearing fault components can be distinguished from other mechanical sources. Gear-mesh frequencies, belt-related vibration, structural resonances, and overlapping spectral components may complicate the interpretation of the envelope spectrum.

Real bearing systems introduce additional effects, including load-dependent contact angles, rolling-element slip, manufacturing tolerances, and speed variation within the analysis window. The model-mismatch experiment in Section 4.13 examined controlled departures from nominal fault orders and showed that geometry-anchored features retained a classification advantage under the specified perturbations. These results provide an initial indication of robustness to kinematic mismatch, while the behavior under independently measured industrial vibration remains a separate validation requirement.

When bearing geometry is unavailable, the characteristic fault orders cannot be calculated with the information required by the present feature extractor. In such cases, alternative representations or methods for estimating the missing physical parameters are necessary. The experiments also showed that machine-level calibration maintained average empirical coverage under parameter perturbations by producing larger prediction sets. Thus, calibration and feature construction should be treated as complementary components rather than interchangeable solutions to inaccurate physical information.

sec.title: 6.4. Study limitations
sec.p: The findings should be interpreted in relation to the controlled simulation design and the assumptions used to generate the vibration signals. The simulator incorporated established bearing fault-frequency relationships, and the geometry-anchored features were constructed using the same underlying kinematic principles. This correspondence allowed the influence of machine geometry to be examined directly, but it also favored representations that explicitly used those relationships. The geometry-perturbation and model-mismatch experiments assessed departures from the nominal assumptions while retaining the principal impulse-response structure of the simulated signals.

The evaluation involved eight simulated machines, with seven source machines available in each leave-one-machine-out experiment. Although this design permitted direct comparisons across machine configurations, the number of independent machine-level units was limited. The reported LMO-CP coverage values therefore describe empirical performance under the evaluated simulation conditions. They do not constitute a general finite-sample guarantee for individual machines or establish the exchangeability of physical machines encountered in industrial applications.

The literature synthesis was structured around selected methodological themes rather than a registered systematic-review protocol. Its purpose was to identify the relationships between evaluation practice, feature representation, distribution shift, and uncertainty calibration. The seven research hypotheses were formalized after the initial experiments, and their assessment should consequently be understood as an exploratory interpretation of the evidence.

The classifier comparison covered histogram-based gradient boosting, logistic regression, random forest, and a small multilayer perceptron. These models provided a basis for examining whether the observed representation effects depended on the classifier family. However, the experiments did not include convolutional networks, transformer-based architectures, or adversarial domain-adaptation models under a common machine-level evaluation protocol. Model-specific hyperparameter optimization was also outside the experimental design.

The unknown-fault analysis considered mechanical looseness as the sole fault category excluded from training. The cost-sensitive decision analysis used one specified cost matrix, while the robustness experiments involved a limited number of random seeds. The resulting observations characterize the selected fault condition, decision assumptions, and perturbation settings rather than the full range of industrial fault mechanisms and maintenance requirements.

Dependence between observations is another consideration. Windows originating from the same recording shared operating and signal-generation parameters, so the number of windows should not be interpreted as the number of independent machine-level observations. The bootstrap intervals and statistical comparisons quantified variation within the simulated evaluation design, but their interpretation remains tied to the available machines and random realizations. Similarly, the fault-line collision audit examined selected bearing geometries under deterministic conditions, while the model-mismatch experiments retained the principal structure of the simulator.

These considerations define the contribution as a controlled methodological investigation of geometry-anchored features, machine-level conformal calibration, and diagnostic performance under specified forms of machine shift. They also establish the experimental conditions that should be addressed when extending the framework to independently collected bearing measurements.

sec.title: 6.5. Future research directions
sec.p: The findings provide a basis for extending the framework from controlled simulation toward experimental and industrial bearing monitoring. Five directions are particularly relevant.
(1) Experimental validation and cross-dataset benchmarking

The first priority is to evaluate the proposed framework using measured bearing vibration signals from datasets such as CWRU, Paderborn, and XJTU-SY. Evaluation should distinguish complete-machine holdout from operating-condition transfer and maintain separation between training and testing recordings. Where available, bearing geometry and operating-condition metadata should be incorporated into feature construction. Comparisons with conventional classifiers, deep-learning models, and representative domain-adaptation methods would allow the observed effects of physically indexed features and machine-level calibration to be examined under measured signal variability.
(2) Evaluation of machine-level coverage across larger equipment populations

The number-of-machines analysis should be extended to include a larger and more heterogeneous population of independent machines. In addition to average coverage, the evaluation should report the distribution of machine-specific coverage, the proportion of machines reaching the nominal target, and the relationship between source-machine diversity and prediction-set size. Such experiments would provide a stronger empirical basis for interpreting conservative calibration and the influence of the number of available machines.
(3) Cost-sensitive conformal decision-making

Future work should investigate the integration of machine-level calibration with conformal risk control [40], allowing diagnostic decisions to be evaluated through operational losses rather than prediction-set coverage alone. Relevant outcomes include missed faults, unnecessary inspections, and maintenance delays. Comparisons across alternative cost matrices and fault prevalences would clarify the circumstances under which uncertainty-aware classification provides a measurable operational advantage.
(4) Unknown-fault recognition under machine shift

The open-set evaluation should be extended beyond mechanical looseness to include additional fault mechanisms and combinations of faults absent from training. Dedicated novelty-detection methods could be examined alongside conformal prediction sets and selective classification. The evaluation should distinguish distribution shift caused by unfamiliar equipment from changes caused by previously unseen fault categories, since both may influence diagnostic confidence.
(5) Hierarchical and group-aware conformal calibration

Further research should examine calibration procedures that explicitly account for the hierarchical organization of vibration observations within recordings and machines. Machine-stratified, hierarchical, and group-conditional methods could be compared with LMO-CP in terms of average coverage, machine-specific reliability, calibration-data requirements, and sensitivity to heterogeneous operating conditions. Particular attention should be given to the assumptions required for finite-sample guarantees when the number of independent machines is small.

Together, these directions establish a progression from experimental validation and larger machine-level evaluations toward uncertainty-aware maintenance decisions and calibration procedures that account for the structure of industrial monitoring data.

sec.title: 7. Conclusions
sec.p: This study investigated cross-machine bearing fault diagnosis by combining geometry-anchored feature representation with machine-level conformal calibration. A structured literature review identified five methodological gaps and seven research hypotheses, which were examined using controlled simulations of eight machines with different bearing geometries, operating speeds, structural resonances, and noise characteristics.

The geometry-anchored representation achieved a leave-one-machine-out classification accuracy of 0.908, compared with 0.585 and 0.575 for frequency-domain and order-domain features. Random window splitting overestimated the accuracy of the fixed-axis representations by as much as 0.29. Feature ablation and the structural fault-line audit showed that the improvement was associated with extracting spectral information at fault-specific kinematic orders. Across the simulated machines, 13 of 24 characteristic fault lines overlapped with lines associated with different faults, explaining an important source of ambiguity in fixed-axis representations.

Machine-level conformal calibration improved average empirical coverage under machine shift. At a nominal coverage level of 0.90, LMO-CP achieved average coverage between approximately 0.90 and 0.93 across the evaluated representations. However, prediction-set informativeness depended strongly on feature construction. Geometry-anchored features produced sets containing approximately one class on average, compared with nearly three classes for the fixed-axis alternatives.

Coverage also varied between individual machines. With geometry-anchored features, worst-machine coverage was 0.751 under pooled LMO-CP and increased to 0.866 under conservative calibration, accompanied by larger prediction sets. The idealized rank argument established the relationship between the number of source machines and the probability of attaining nominal machine-level coverage under its stated assumptions. The robustness experiments further showed that the geometry-anchored representation retained its classification advantage under controlled kinematic mismatch and across alternative classifiers, although worst-machine coverage decreased under more demanding signal conditions.

The unknown-fault and decision analyses identified separate requirements for industrial application. Approximately 70% of unknown mechanical-looseness windows were classified as normal, while the evaluated novelty-detection and abstention procedures did not produce consistent operational improvements under the selected conditions. These findings distinguish reliable classification among known faults from the broader requirements of unknown-fault recognition and maintenance decision-making.

The study establishes a controlled evaluation framework in which diagnostic accuracy, prediction-set coverage, machine-specific reliability, and prediction-set size are assessed together. Its principal contribution is the joint examination of physically indexed fault features and calibration based on machine-level holdouts. The resulting evidence supports the use of machine-level evaluation and physically meaningful feature construction when developing diagnostic models for unfamiliar equipment. Experimental validation using independent bearing measurements remains necessary to establish how these findings translate to industrial operating conditions.

Recording severity is exp(U(ln0.9, ln2.6)) divided by a difficulty factor (0.5 in the reference experiments, 0.4 and 0.7 for the noise sensitivity runs), multiplied by noise level and gain. Speed fluctuation across recordings is 4% (SD). Gradient-boosting classifiers use random_state equal to the seed (nested models add the held-out machine index). The domain classifier for weighted conformal prediction is class-balanced logistic regression with C = 0.5. The number of experiments is small enough to run on a single central processing unit (CPU) core in under ten minutes per seed. The experiments were implemented in Python using scikit-learn. The Python and scikit-learn versions, together with the remaining software dependencies, are documented in the supplementary implementation files.
